claims.evidence: This is supported by expansion microscopy images shown in Figure 2E5, E6, and F6.

claims.claim: The levels of Kv3.1 staining in the WT are higher than in the Kv3.3KO.
claims.source: While the calyceal Kv3.3 staining in the WT is similar to that in the Kv3.1KO, the levels of Kv3.1 staining in the WT are higher (than in the Kv3.3KO) consistent with the hypothesis that Kv3.1 may gain access to the presynaptic compartment through heteromeric assembly with Kv3.3 subunits.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on comparison of immunostaining patterns shown in Figure 2.

claims.claim: Kv3.1 may gain access to the presynaptic compartment through heteromeric assembly with Kv3.3 subunits.
claims.source: While the calyceal Kv3.3 staining in the WT is similar to that in the Kv3.1KO, the levels of Kv3.1 staining in the WT are higher (than in the Kv3.3KO) consistent with the hypothesis that Kv3.1 may gain access to the presynaptic compartment through heteromeric assembly with Kv3.3 subunits.
claims.evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the immunostaining patterns and represents speculation about the mechanism.

claims.claim: Only Kv3.3 subunits are required to achieve trafficking of Kv3 channels to the presynaptic terminal.
claims.source: This data shows that while both Kv3.1 and Kv3.3 subunits are present in the postsynaptic soma membrane, only Kv3.3 subunits are required to achieve trafficking of Kv3 channels to the presynaptic terminal; and there is some evidence that the presence of Kv3.3 permits access of Kv3.1 subunits to the terminal, while both Kv3.1 and Kv3.3 were localised to the postsynaptic plasma membrane in the WT tissue.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the differential localization patterns observed in the knockout mice shown in Figure 2.

claims.claim: The presence of Kv3.3 permits access of Kv3.1 subunits to the terminal.
claims.source: This data shows that while both Kv3.1 and Kv3.3 subunits are present in the postsynaptic soma membrane, only Kv3.3 subunits are required to achieve trafficking of Kv3 channels to the presynaptic terminal; and there is some evidence that the presence of Kv3.3 permits access of Kv3.1 subunits to the terminal, while both Kv3.1 and Kv3.3 were localised to the postsynaptic plasma membrane in the WT tissue.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that Kv3.1 staining is higher in WT than in Kv3.3KO presynaptic terminals.

claims.claim: Both Kv3.1 and Kv3.3 were localised to the postsynaptic plasma membrane in the WT tissue.
claims.source: This data shows that while both Kv3.1 and Kv3.3 subunits are present in the postsynaptic soma membrane, only Kv3.3 subunits are required to achieve trafficking of Kv3 channels to the presynaptic terminal; and there is some evidence that the presence of Kv3.3 permits access of Kv3.1 subunits to the terminal, while both Kv3.1 and Kv3.3 were localised to the postsynaptic plasma membrane in the WT tissue.
claims.evidence: This is supported by expansion microscopy images shown in Figure 2.

claims.claim: The calyceal EPSCs recorded from Kv3.3KO mice were of larger peak amplitude compared to WT or Kv3.1KOs.
claims.source: The calyceal EPSCs recorded from Kv3.3KO mice were of larger peak amplitude and longer lasting compared to WT or Kv3.1KOs, consistent with increased transmitter release from the calyx of Held in the Kv3.3KO.
claims.evidence: This is supported by EPSC amplitude data shown in Figure 3B.

claims.claim: The calyceal EPSCs recorded from Kv3.3KO mice were longer lasting compared to WT or Kv3.1KOs.
claims.source: The calyceal EPSCs recorded from Kv3.3KO mice were of larger peak amplitude and longer lasting compared to WT or Kv3.1KOs, consistent with increased transmitter release from the calyx of Held in the Kv3.3KO.
claims.evidence: This is supported by EPSC decay tau data shown in Figure 3D.

claims.claim: Larger and longer lasting EPSCs in Kv3.3KO are consistent with increased transmitter release from the calyx of Held.
claims.source: The calyceal EPSCs recorded from Kv3.3KO mice were of larger peak amplitude and longer lasting compared to WT or Kv3.1KOs, consistent with increased transmitter release from the calyx of Held in the Kv3.3KO.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the EPSC characteristics shown in Figure 3.

claims.claim: EPSC amplitudes were similar in WT (–13±2 nA) and Kv3.1KO (–14±2 nA).
claims.source: EPSC amplitudes were similar in WT and Kv3.1KO, –13±2 nA (n=21) and –14±2 nA (n=17), respectively; but increased significantly in the Kv3.3KO to –18±5 nA (n=21; one-way ANOVA, Tukey's post hoc, Kv3.3KO vs WT, p=0.0001; Kv3.3KO vs Kv3.1KO p=0.0005).
claims.evidence: This is supported by EPSC amplitude data shown in Figure 3B.

claims.claim: EPSC amplitude increased significantly in the Kv3.3KO to –18±5 nA.
claims.source: EPSC amplitudes were similar in WT and Kv3.1KO, –13±2 nA (n=21) and –14±2 nA (n=17), respectively; but increased significantly in the Kv3.3KO to –18±5 nA (n=21; one-way ANOVA, Tukey's post hoc, Kv3.3KO vs WT, p=0.0001; Kv3.3KO vs Kv3.1KO p=0.0005).
claims.evidence: This is supported by EPSC amplitude data shown in Figure 3B.

claims.claim: The decay tau for the EPSCs in the Kv3.3KO slowed to 0.23±0.06ms compared to 0.17±0.04ms in WT.
claims.source: The decay tau for the EPSCs in the Kv3.3KO slowed to 0.23±0.06ms (n=21) compared to 0.17±0.04ms in WT (n=21; one-way ANOVA, Tukey's post hoc, p=0.0012).
claims.evidence: This is supported by EPSC decay tau data shown in Figure 3D.

claims.claim: The total charge of EPSCs in Kv3.3KOs increased to –10±4 nC compared to –6±1 nC in WT.
claims.source: The total charge of EPSCs in Kv3.3KOs increased to –10±4 nC (n=21) compared to –6±1 nC and –7±2 nC in WT (n=21) and Kv3.1KOs (n=17), respectively (one-way ANOVA, Tukey's post hoc; Kv3.3KO vs WT, p=0.0001; Kv3.3KO vs Kv3.1KO p=0.0007).
claims.evidence: This is supported by EPSC charge data shown in Figure 3E.

claims.claim: No change of EPSC rise time was observed in either KO.
claims.source: No change of EPSC rise time was observed in either KO (one-way ANOVA, p=0.1918).
claims.evidence: This is supported by EPSC rise time data shown in Figure 3C.

claims.claim: There was a small significant decrease in mEPSC quantal amplitude in the Kv3.3KO relative to WT.
claims.source: Examination of miniature EPSCs in postsynaptic MNTB neurons from each genotype (Figure 3—figure supplement 1) showed no difference in the mEPSC frequency, rise-time or decay tau. There was a small significant decrease in quantal amplitude in the Kv3.3KO relative to WT, but no change in the Kv3.1KO.
claims.evidence: This is supported by mEPSC data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: There was no change in mEPSC quantal amplitude in the Kv3.1KO.
claims.source: Examination of miniature EPSCs in postsynaptic MNTB neurons from each genotype (Figure 3—figure supplement 1) showed no difference in the mEPSC frequency, rise-time or decay tau. There was a small significant decrease in quantal amplitude in the Kv3.3KO relative to WT, but no change in the Kv3.1KO.
claims.evidence: This is supported by mEPSC data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: The decreased mEPSC amplitude in Kv3.3KO perhaps reflects an opposing change in synaptic scaling due to the larger transmitter release.
claims.source: This contrasts with the increased amplitude of the evoked EPSCs in the Kv3.3KO measured here, and perhaps reflects an opposing change in synaptic scaling due to the larger transmitter release induced in the Kv3.3KO (Tatavarty et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: This is speculation about the mechanism, supported by citation to Tatavarty et al., 2013.

claims.claim: Blocking presynaptic Kv3 channels with TEA had a much smaller effect on EPSC amplitude in the Kv3.3 KO compared to WT and Kv3.1 KO.
claims.source: Indeed, blocking Kv3 channels with TEA had a much smaller effect on EPSC amplitude in the Kv3.3 KO compared to WT and Kv3.1 KO.
claims.evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3F–H.

claims.claim: TEA increased EPSC amplitude to 160% ± 33% in WT, compared to 114% ± 6% in Kv3.3KO.
claims.source: TEA increased EPSC amplitude to 160% ± 33% (n=8) in WT, compared to 114% ± 6% (n=6) in Kv3.3KO (Kruskal-Wallis, Dunn's multiple comparison, p=0.0031).
claims.evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3H.

claims.claim: The EPSC amplitude in the Kv3.1KO (136% ± 11%) was not significantly different from WT in response to TEA.
claims.source: The EPSC amplitude in the Kv3.1KO (136% ± 11%, n=4) was not significantly different from WT (Kruskal-Wallis, Dunn's multiple comparison p=0.99).
claims.evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3H.

claims.claim: The reduced TEA effect in Kv3.3KO is consistent with dominance of presynaptic repolarisation by channels containing Kv3.3.
claims.source: This result is consistent with dominance of presynaptic repolarisation by channels containing Kv3.3.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the TEA data shown in Figure 3F–H.

claims.claim: The calyx of Held/MNTB synapse is capable of sustained transmission at firing frequencies of around 300 Hz in vivo.
claims.source: The calyx of Held/MNTB synapse is capable of sustained transmission at firing frequencies of around 300 Hz in vivo (Kopp-Scheinpflug et al., 2008) (also see Figure 8), encoding information about sound stimuli for binaural integration with high temporal precision.
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to Kopp-Scheinpflug et al., 2008 and by in vivo data shown in Figure 8.

claims.claim: The calyx of Held giant synapse can sustain short AP bursts with peak firing rates of up to 1000 Hz in vitro for a few milliseconds.
claims.source: Indeed, the calyx of Held giant synapse can sustain short AP bursts with peak firing rates of up to 1000 Hz, in vitro (Kim et al., 2013) for a few milliseconds.
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to Kim et al., 2013.

claims.claim: The first EPSC amplitude in trains delivered to the calyx/MNTB from the Kv3.3KO mouse was of larger amplitude than observed in WT or in the Kv3.1KO.
claims.source: The first EPSC amplitude in trains delivered to the calyx/MNTB from the Kv3.3KO mouse was of larger amplitude than observed in WT or in the Kv3.1KO and subsequent EPSCs showed a larger short-term depression.
claims.evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4A–C.

claims.claim: Subsequent EPSCs in Kv3.3KO showed a larger short-term depression than WT or Kv3.1KO.
claims.source: The first EPSC amplitude in trains delivered to the calyx/MNTB from the Kv3.3KO mouse was of larger amplitude than observed in WT or in the Kv3.1KO and subsequent EPSCs showed a larger short-term depression.
claims.evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4A–C and quantified in Figure 4D.

claims.claim: Paired pulse ratio (PPR) was significantly decreased in the Kv3.3KO compared to both WT and Kv3.1KO at 100 Hz, 200 Hz, and 600 Hz.
claims.source: Paired pulse ratio (PPR) was significantly decreased in the Kv3.3KO compared to both WT and Kv3.1KO at 100 Hz, 200 Hz, and 600 Hz, with mean PPR (EPSC2/EPSC1) plotted in Figure 4D (left column).
claims.evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4D and Table 1.

claims.claim: Enhanced depression of EPSC amplitude was maintained for the duration of the train in Kv3.3KO.
claims.source: This enhanced depression of EPSC amplitude was maintained for the duration of the train shown in comparison with the 80th EPSC in the train (EPSC80/EPSC1; Figure 4D, right column; Table 1).
claims.evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4D and Table 1.

claims.claim: The Kv3.3KO consistently showed the fastest rate of short-term depression, compared to WT and Kv3.1KOs.
claims.source: The Kv3.3KO consistently showed the fastest rate of short-term depression, compared to WT and Kv3.1KOs; this was highly significant at 100 Hz and 200 Hz (Table 1).
claims.evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4E–G and Table 1.

claims.claim: The decay time-constant for short-term depression at 600 Hz was 6±1ms for Kv3.3KOs, 11±2ms for WT and 20±13ms for Kv3.1KOs.
claims.source: The decay time-constant for short-term depression was 6±1ms for Kv3.3KOs (n=8), 11±2ms for WT (n=10) and 20±13ms for Kv3.1KOs (n=5; Table 1).
claims.evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4G and Table 1.

claims.claim: At all frequencies, EPSCs from the Kv3.3KO mice showed lower amplitude steady-state values in comparison to WT.
claims.source: At all frequencies, EPSCs from the Kv3.3KO mice showed lower amplitude steady-state values in comparison to WT; while the Kv3.1KO data was either the same or greater than WT (Figure 4E, Table 1).
claims.evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4E–G and Table 1.

claims.claim: Presynaptic spike broadening has been shown to enhance vesicle recycling during repetitive stimulation trains due to enhanced calcium-dependent recovery.
claims.source: Presynaptic spike broadening has previously been shown to enhance vesicle recycling during repetitive stimulation trains (Wang and Kaczmarek, 1998) due to enhanced calcium-dependent recovery.
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to Wang and Kaczmarek, 1998.

claims.claim: The fast time-constant of recovery was significantly accelerated in the Kv3.3KO (0.2±0.2 s) compared to WT (0.45±0.2 s) and Kv3.1KO (0.4±0.2 s).
claims.source: The fast time-constant was significantly accelerated in the Kv3.3KO compared to WT and Kv3.1KO (0.2±0.2 s in Kv3.3KO; 0.45±0.2 s in WT and 0.4±0.2 s in the Kv3.1KO; Figure 5F, p=0.025).
claims.evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5F.

claims.claim: The slow time-constant of recovery was 5±3 s in WT, and was similar to both Kv3.1KO and Kv3.3KO.
claims.source: The slow time-constant was 5±3 s in WT, and was similar to both Kv3.1KO and Kv3.3KO (Figure 5G).
claims.evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5G.

claims.claim: The enhanced fast recovery rate is consistent with an activity-dependent component of vesicle recycling.
claims.source: The enhanced fast recovery rate is consistent with an activity-dependent component of vesicle recycling as observed previously on blocking presynaptic Kv3 channels at the calyx of Held (Wang and Kaczmarek, 1998) and as recently attributed to Ca2+-phospholipid-dependent vesicle priming (Lipstein et al., 2021) via Munc13-1.
claims.evidence: This is an inference supported by citations to Wang and Kaczmarek, 1998 and Lipstein et al., 2021.

claims.claim: The dominant change in the model parameters between WT and Kv3.3KO was an increase in the probability of vesicular release (Pv) from 0.13 in WT to 0.266 in the Kv3.3KO.
claims.source: The table in Figure 6B shows that the dominant change in the model parameters between WT and Kv3.3KO, was an increase in the probability of vesicular release (Pv) from 0.13 in WT to 0.266 in the Kv3.3KO.
claims.evidence: This is supported by computational modeling results shown in Figure 6B.

claims.claim: There was a 20% acceleration of the replenishment rate (smaller τh) in Kv3.3KO.
claims.source: There was also evidence for an increase in activity-dependent recycling, with a 20% acceleration of the replenishment rate (smaller τh in Kv3.3KO).
claims.evidence: This is supported by computational modeling results shown in Figure 6B.

claims.claim: The physiologically observed changes in short-term depression and recycling could be fit across the range of stimuli rates with only two parameter changes in the Kv3.3KO: a dramatically increased Pv and a modest decrease in the activity-dependent vesicle recycling time-constant τh.
claims.source: This model showed that the physiologically observed changes in short-term depression and recycling could be fit across the range of stimuli rates with only two parameter changes in the Kv3.3KO: a dramatically increased Pv and a modest decrease in the activity-dependent vesicle recycling time-constant τh (higher recycling rate), both of which are attributable to the raised calcium influx during the presynaptic AP (see Neher and Sakaba, 2008; Young and Veeraraghavan, 2021).
claims.evidence: This is supported by computational modeling results shown in Figure 6 and represents an inference about the mechanism.

claims.claim: Both increased Pv and decreased τh are attributable to the raised calcium influx during the presynaptic AP.
claims.source: This model showed that the physiologically observed changes in short-term depression and recycling could be fit across the range of stimuli rates with only two parameter changes in the Kv3.3KO: a dramatically increased Pv and a modest decrease in the activity-dependent vesicle recycling time-constant τh (higher recycling rate), both of which are attributable to the raised calcium influx during the presynaptic AP (see Neher and Sakaba, 2008; Young and Veeraraghavan, 2021).
claims.evidence: This is an inference supported by citations to Neher and Sakaba, 2008; Young and Veeraraghavan, 2021.

claims.claim: MNTB AP output in response to high frequency calyceal EPSC input declines with both Kv3.1 and Kv3.3 deletion.
claims.source: The initial observation was that MNTB AP output in response to high frequency calyceal EPSC input, declines with both Kv3.1 and Kv3.3 deletion (Figure 7A) when measured over the whole train (WT: 52.49% ± 8.15%, n=5; Kv3.3KO: 29.8% ± 10.43%, n=7; Kv3.1KO: 36.29% ± 11.12%, n=6; Kv3.3KO vs WT p=0.0044, Kv3.1KO vs WT p=0.046, one-way ANOVA, Tukey's post hoc).
claims.evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 7A.

claims.claim: There are three phases of AP firing to evoked trains of calyceal synaptic responses.
claims.source: But closer inspection reveals three phases of AP firing to evoked trains of calyceal synaptic responses as illustrated in Figure 7B.
claims.evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 7B.

claims.claim: In Phase I, every evoked EPSP triggered one MNTB AP.
claims.source: In Phase I (green trace, Figure 7B) which predominates at the start of each train, every evoked EPSP triggered one MNTB AP: so the MNTB output matched the calyx input.
claims.evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 7B.

claims.claim: In Phase II, EPSPs often failed to evoke an AP, and the MNTB AP firing becomes chaotic and unpredictable.
claims.source: Firing then transitioned to Phase II (blue trace, Figure 7B) after around 6–9 stimuli, where EPSPs often failed to evoke an AP, and the MNTB AP firing becomes chaotic, unpredictable and poorly transmits the timing information contained within the presynaptic AP train.
claims.evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 7B.

claims.claim: In Phase III, the MNTB neuron fired APs to alternate EPSPs.
claims.source: In Phase III (black trace, Figure 7B): the EPSP had undergone short-term depression and approached a 'steady-state' amplitude; now the MNTB neuron fired APs to alternate EPSPs.
claims.evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 7B.

claims.claim: At frequencies up to 200 Hz the duration of Phase I was essentially identical across the three genotypes.
claims.source: At frequencies up to 200 Hz the duration of Phase I was essentially identical across the three genotypes (Figure 7C), all showed 100% firing throughout the train; then from 300 Hz and above, the Phase I duration declined dramatically for all genotypes.
claims.evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 7C.

claims.claim: At 600 Hz stimulation frequency, only 1 out of 6 calyx/MNTB pairs in Kv3.3KO briefly entered Phase III firing.
claims.source: The latency for Phase III was similar in WT and Kv3.1KO (510±224ms and 597±251ms, respectively) but in the Kv3.3KO only 1 out of 6 calyx/MNTB pairs briefly entered Phase III firing (Kv3.3KO vs WT Phase II p=0.0135, Phase III p=0.02, two-way ANOVA, Tukey's post hoc).
claims.evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 7D.

claims.claim: Presynaptic Kv3.3 and fast presynaptic APs serve a role in maintaining information transmission across the synapse during high frequency firing.
claims.source: This is consistent with the idea that presynaptic Kv3.3 and hence fast presynaptic APs, serve a role in maintaining information transmission across the synapse during high frequency firing, when short APs conserve resources, and slow the rate of short-term depression.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the Phase III firing data shown in Figure 7D.

claims.claim: In the Kv3.1KO, calyceal stimulation evoked a sustained depolarisation at frequencies above 100 Hz.
claims.source: However, in the Kv3.1KO, calyceal stimulation evoked a sustained depolarisation (in addition to EPSPs) at frequencies above 100 Hz (Figure 7E).
claims.evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 7E.

claims.claim: The plateau depolarisation was significantly larger for the Kv3.1KO at frequencies above 100 Hz.
claims.source: Although all genotypes exhibited this plateau depolarisation at 600 Hz, it was significantly larger for the Kv3.1KO at frequencies above 100 Hz (Figure 7F).
claims.evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 7F.

claims.claim: Kv3.3KOs showed a reduced plateau potential at frequencies above 300 Hz, reaching significance only at 600 Hz.
claims.source: In contrast, Kv3.3KOs showed a reduced plateau potential at frequencies above 300 Hz, reaching significance only at 600 Hz (Figure 7F; two-way ANOVA, Tukey's post hoc).
claims.evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 7F.

claims.claim: The time to half-decay of the depolarisation following the end of the train was significantly longer in the Kv3.1KO (15.96±8.59ms) compared to WT (2.79±1.73ms).
claims.source: This was also observed as a decaying depolarisation at the end of the train (Figure 7G), with the time to half-decay plotted in Figure 7H (WT: 2.79±1.73ms, n=7: Kv3.3KO: 1.89±0.92ms, n=6: Kv3.1KO: 15.96±8.59ms, n=8: Kv3.1KO vs WT p=0. 000553, one-way ANOVA, Tukey's post hoc).
claims.evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 7H.

claims.claim: In WT and Kv3.3KO genotypes, the decay of depolarisation was similar to the postsynaptic membrane time-constant.
claims.source: In WT and Kv3.3KO genotypes, this decay was similar to the postsynaptic membrane time-constant, but in the Kv3.1KO, non-synchronous spontaneous EPSPs were observed.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on comparison of decay kinetics with membrane time constants.

claims.claim: In the Kv3.1KO, non-synchronous spontaneous EPSPs were observed.
claims.source: In WT and Kv3.3KO genotypes, this decay was similar to the postsynaptic membrane time-constant, but in the Kv3.1KO, non-synchronous spontaneous EPSPs were observed.
claims.evidence: This is supported by observation of the data shown in Figure 7G.

claims.claim: The EPSC decay time constants for all genotypes were essentially identical.
claims.source: The EPSC decay time constants for all genotypes were essentially identical, consistent with no change in glutamate receptor expression (WT: 2.74±1.26ms, n=8; Kv3.3KO: 3.1±0.87ms, n=8; Kv3.1KO: 3.54±0.9ms, n=6).
claims.evidence: This is supported by EPSC decay time constant measurements.

claims.claim: Auditory Brainstem Response (ABR) thresholds were similar in 6-month-old WT and Kv3.3KO mice.
claims.source: Behaviourally, the Kv3.3KO mouse is as sensitive to sound as the WT in that Auditory Brainstem Response (ABR) thresholds were similar in 6-month-old WT and Kv3.3KO mice, with no statistical difference across a wide frequency range (see summary statistics, unpaired t-test with Holm-Šídák's test for multiple comparisons).
claims.evidence: This is supported by ABR threshold measurements.

claims.claim: ABR waveform analysis showed significant deficits in Wave IV at 6 months in Kv3.3KO which were not apparent at 1 month of age.
claims.source: However, further analysis of the ABR waveform showed significant deficits in Wave IV at 6 months which were not apparent in recordings taken at 1 month of age.
claims.evidence: This is supported by ABR waveform analysis.

claims.claim: A developmental 'knockout' of the MNTB impacts ABR Wave III.
claims.source: We have previously demonstrated that a developmental 'knockout' of the MNTB impacts ABR Wave III (Jalabi et al., 2013), so the decrease in Wave IV reflects changes in downstream areas of the auditory brainstem and is being characterized as part of another study.
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to Jalabi et al., 2013.

claims.claim: The decrease in ABR Wave IV reflects changes in downstream areas of the auditory brainstem.
claims.source: We have previously demonstrated that a developmental 'knockout' of the MNTB impacts ABR Wave III (Jalabi et al., 2013), so the decrease in Wave IV reflects changes in downstream areas of the auditory brainstem and is being characterized as part of another study.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the known anatomy and the ABR data.

claims.claim: AP halfwidth of the presynaptic AP was significantly longer in Kv3.3KOs (0.25ms) compared to WT recordings (0.17ms).
claims.source: AP halfwidth of the presynaptic AP (preAP) was significantly longer in Kv3.3KOs (0.25ms [0.16; 0.31]; n=13) compared to WT recordings (0.17ms [0.16; 0.19]; n=20; Figure 8B; Mann-Whitney Rank Sum Test: p=0.036).
claims.evidence: This is supported by in vivo extracellular recording data shown in Figure 8B.

claims.claim: Synaptic delays were significantly prolonged in Kv3.3KOs (0.56ms) compared to WT controls (0.44ms).
claims.source: Synaptic delays as measured by peak-to-peak times in the complex waveform were also significantly prolonged in Kv3.3KOs (0.56ms [0.45; 0.70]; n=13) compared to WT controls (0.44ms [0.41; 0.49]; n=20; Figure 8C; n=13; Mann-Whitney Rank Sum Test: p=0.013).
claims.evidence: This is supported by in vivo extracellular recording data shown in Figure 8C.

claims.claim: Postsynaptic AP duration was prolonged in the Kv3.3KOs (0.64ms) compared to WT (0.36ms).
claims.source: While changes in presynaptic AP duration and synaptic delay may predominantly affect temporal processing, the prolonged postsynaptic AP duration observed in the Kv3.3KOs (0.64ms [0.29; 0.46]; n=13; Figure 8D) might influence high-frequency firing abilities (WT: 0.36ms [0.48; 0.82]; n=20; Mann-Whitney Rank Sum Test: p≤0.001).

results.result: Kv3.1 and Kv3.3 are highly expressed in the auditory brainstem, specifically in the cochlear nucleus and MNTB, with Kv3.3 representing approximately 52% of Kv3 mRNA in the cochlear nucleus.
results.evaluation: Claims C2, C45, C47-C52 are supported by mRNA sequencing data (Figure 1—figure supplement 1) and immunohistochemistry (Figure 1—figure supplements 2 and 3). The quantitative mRNA data provides specific percentages for each Kv3 subunit, with Kv3.3 being the predominant subunit at 52.0% ± 6.0%.

results.result: Kv3.3 is specifically localized to presynaptic terminals at the calyx of Held, while Kv3.1 shows minimal presynaptic localization. Expansion microscopy demonstrates that Kv3.3 is present on both release and non-release faces of the presynaptic terminal, and that Kv3.3 is required for presynaptic Kv3 channel trafficking.
results.evaluation: Claims C3, C42, C72-C84 are strongly supported by expansion microscopy data in Figure 2. The high-resolution imaging clearly shows differential localization patterns: Kv3.3 is present in presynaptic terminals in Kv3.1KO tissue, but Kv3.1 shows little presynaptic labeling in Kv3.3KO tissue. This demonstrates that Kv3.3 is necessary and sufficient for presynaptic Kv3 channel localization.

results.result: Deletion of Kv3.3 significantly increases presynaptic action potential duration at the calyx of Held (from 0.28±0.02ms to 0.43±0.03ms at half-width), while deletion of Kv3.1 has minimal effect on AP duration. TEA treatment phenocopies the Kv3.3KO effect.
results.evaluation: Claims C4, C54-C66 are supported by direct electrophysiological measurements in Figure 1. The data show statistically significant increases in AP half-width in Kv3.3KO (p=0.0042) and with TEA treatment (p=0.0016), but not in Kv3.1KO. The decay slope is significantly slowed in both Kv3.3KO and TEA conditions, while other AP parameters (rise slope, threshold, membrane resistance) remain unchanged, indicating specificity of the effect.

results.result: Deletion of Kv3.3 increases excitatory transmitter release at the calyx of Held, with EPSC amplitudes increasing from -13±2 nA in WT to -18±5 nA in Kv3.3KO. TEA has a reduced effect on EPSC amplitude in Kv3.3KO (114% ± 6%) compared to WT (160% ± 33%), indicating that Kv3.3 dominates presynaptic repolarization.
results.evaluation: Claims C5, C43, C85-C92, C96-C99 are supported by EPSC measurements in Figure 3. The increased EPSC amplitude in Kv3.3KO is statistically significant (p=0.0001 vs WT), and the occlusion of TEA effect in Kv3.3KO (p=0.0031 vs WT) provides strong evidence that Kv3.3-containing channels are the primary mediators of presynaptic repolarization. The lack of effect in Kv3.1KO further supports the specificity.

results.result: Deletion of Kv3.3 enhances short-term depression during high-frequency transmission (100-600 Hz), with faster depression kinetics and lower steady-state EPSC amplitudes. The paired-pulse ratio is significantly decreased in Kv3.3KO at all tested frequencies, and the decay time constant for depression at 600 Hz is reduced from 11±2ms in WT to 6±1ms in Kv3.3KO.
results.evaluation: Claims C6, C102-C108 are supported by extensive data in Figure 4 and Table 1. The enhanced short-term depression is demonstrated across multiple frequencies with statistically significant differences in paired-pulse ratios, decay time constants, and steady-state amplitudes. The consistency of the phenotype across different stimulation frequencies strengthens the conclusion.

results.result: The fast time-constant of recovery from short-term depression is significantly accelerated in Kv3.3KO (0.2±0.2 s) compared to WT (0.45±0.2 s), while the slow time-constant remains unchanged. This enhanced fast recovery is consistent with activity-dependent vesicle recycling.
results.evaluation: Claims C110-C112 are supported by recovery data in Figure 5. The acceleration of the fast recovery component is statistically significant (p=0.025), while the slow component shows no difference between genotypes. The interpretation linking this to activity-dependent recycling is reasonable given the citations to Wang and Kaczmarek, 1998 and Lipstein et al., 2021, though the mechanism is inferred rather than directly demonstrated.

results.result: Computational modeling shows that the enhanced EPSC and short-term depression in Kv3.3KO can be explained by a two-fold increase in vesicle release probability (Pv from 0.13 to 0.266) and a 20% acceleration of activity-dependent vesicle replenishment (τh from 66.9 to 52.2 ms).
results.evaluation: Claims C11-C12, C113-C116, C152-C153 are supported by computational modeling in Figure 6. The model successfully fits the experimental data across multiple stimulation frequencies (100-600 Hz) with only two parameter changes. However, this is a model-based inference rather than direct measurement. The model assumes specific mechanisms (e.g., single readily releasable pool, fixed pool size) that may not fully capture the biological complexity. The conclusion that both parameters are attributable to increased calcium influx (C116) is reasonable but indirect.

results.result: MNTB neurons exhibit three distinct phases of firing in response to high-frequency synaptic input: Phase I (1:1 fidelity), Phase II (chaotic firing with failures), and Phase III (firing to alternate stimuli). In Kv3.3KO, neurons fail to reach Phase III at 600 Hz, with only 1 of 6 calyx/MNTB pairs briefly entering this phase.
results.evaluation: Claims C117-C124 are supported by data in Figure 7. The three-phase firing pattern is clearly demonstrated in Figure 7B, and the quantification in Figure 7C-D shows that Kv3.3KO neurons have significantly reduced ability to enter Phase III (p=0.02). This suggests impaired stability of synaptic transmission at high frequencies. The interpretation that presynaptic Kv3.3 maintains information transmission (C124) is a reasonable inference from the data.

results.result: In vivo recordings show that Kv3.3KO mice have delayed responses to sound (first spike latency increased from 3.44ms to 4.06ms), higher spontaneous firing (16.5 Hz to 40 Hz), lower evoked firing rates (350 Hz to 240 Hz), and reduced signal-to-noise ratio (9.70 to 2.77).
results.evaluation: Claims C7-C10, C136-C144 are supported by in vivo extracellular recordings in Figure 8. All reported changes are statistically significant with appropriate non-parametric tests (Mann-Whitney Rank Sum Test). The data demonstrate functional consequences of Kv3.3 deletion on auditory processing. However, the increased spontaneous firing (C8, C143) may reflect upstream effects in the auditory pathway rather than direct MNTB effects, as acknowledged by the authors (C218).

results.result: ABR thresholds are similar between WT and Kv3.3KO mice at 6 months, but Wave IV shows significant deficits at 6 months that were not present at 1 month. The decrease in Wave IV reflects changes in downstream auditory brainstem areas rather than direct MNTB effects.
results.evaluation: Claims C132-C135 are supported by ABR measurements, though the data are not shown in the provided figures. The interpretation that Wave IV changes reflect downstream effects (C135) is based on previous work (Jalabi et al., 2013) showing that MNTB knockout affects Wave III. This is a reasonable inference but represents an indirect conclusion. The age-dependent emergence of Wave IV deficits suggests progressive or compensatory changes.

results.result: Kv3.1KO mice show a sustained depolarization plateau during high-frequency stimulation (>100 Hz) that is significantly larger than in WT or Kv3.3KO. The time to half-decay of this depolarization is significantly longer in Kv3.1KO (15.96±8.59ms) compared to WT (2.79±1.73ms).
results.evaluation: Claims C125-C131 are supported by data in Figure 7E-H. The plateau depolarization in Kv3.1KO is statistically significant at frequencies above 100 Hz, and the prolonged decay (p=0.000553) is accompanied by non-synchronous spontaneous EPSPs. This phenotype is distinct from Kv3.3KO and suggests a postsynaptic role for Kv3.1. However, this finding led the authors to focus on Kv3.3KO for in vivo experiments, limiting the interpretation of Kv3.1's role.

results.result: Kv3.3 mediates fast repolarization for short precise APs, conserving transmission during sustained high-frequency activity at the calyx of Held synapse. Presynaptic Kv3.3 subunits are essential for fast AP repolarization, improved temporal accuracy, and conservation of presynaptic resources during high-frequency firing.
results.evaluation: Claims C13, C44, C145-C149, C227-C230 represent the main conclusions of the study, integrating multiple lines of evidence: localization (Figure 2), AP duration (Figure 1), transmitter release (Figure 3), short-term depression (Figures 4-5), modeling (Figure 6), postsynaptic firing (Figure 7), and in vivo function (Figure 8). The convergence of these independent approaches strongly supports the conclusion that Kv3.3 is critical for presynaptic function at this synapse. The generalization to 'fast synapses' (C230) is reasonable but extends beyond the direct evidence.

results.result: Background on Kv3 channels: Kv3 channels mediate rapid AP repolarization, are expressed throughout the brain, have four gene family members that assemble as tetramers, display ultra-fast kinetics with half-activation at positive voltages, and show functional redundancy in knockout studies.
results.evaluation: Claims C1, C14-C33 represent established knowledge about Kv3 channels supported by extensive citations to prior literature. These claims provide necessary background context but do not represent novel findings of this study. The citations are appropriate and the statements are consistent with the established literature.

results.result: Background on the calyx of Held synapse: Changes in presynaptic AP waveform control calcium influx and neurotransmitter release, influencing short-term plasticity. The calyx of Held synapse is optimized for speed and fidelity, operating at the 'biophysical limit' of information processing for binaural sound localization.
results.evaluation: Claims C34-C41 represent established knowledge about the calyx of Held synapse supported by appropriate citations. These provide important context for understanding why this synapse is an ideal model system for studying presynaptic Kv3 function. The characterization as operating at the 'biophysical limit' (C41) is supported by multiple citations.

results.result: Prior literature on Kv3 localization: Low concentrations of TEA (1 mM) selectively block Kv3 channels. Kv3.1b is present at the non-release face of the calyx of Held, while Kv3.3 is present at the release face. Kv3.3 has been demonstrated at various synaptic terminals including vestibular nuclei, neuromuscular junction, and hippocampal mossy fibers.
results.evaluation: Claims C53, C67-C71 represent prior knowledge supported by appropriate citations. The TEA selectivity (C53) is established pharmacology. The differential localization of Kv3.1b and Kv3.3 (C67-C68) from prior EM studies provides important context for the expansion microscopy results in this study. The widespread distribution of Kv3.3 at terminals (C69-C71) suggests general relevance of the findings.

results.result: Speculative claims about mechanisms: Kv3.1 may gain access to presynaptic compartments through heteromeric assembly with Kv3.3; decreased mEPSC amplitude may reflect synaptic scaling; Kv3.3 inactivation may be suppressed by Hax1; presynaptic Kv3.3 may enhance resource conservation and support nanodomain architecture; SCA13 mutations may disrupt interaural level discrimination.
results.evaluation: Claims C81, C95, C166, C173, C185, C203, C222-C223, C225-C226 represent speculative interpretations or hypotheses that extend beyond the direct evidence. While these are reasonable hypotheses supported by citations or the current data, they require additional experiments for validation. For example, the heteromeric assembly hypothesis (C81) is plausible but not directly tested, and the SCA13 implications (C225-C226) are extrapolations from the knockout data.

results.result: Miniature EPSC analysis shows a small significant decrease in quantal amplitude in Kv3.3KO relative to WT, but no change in Kv3.1KO. There were no differences in mEPSC frequency, rise-time, or decay tau between genotypes.
results.evaluation: Claims C93-C94 are supported by data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1. The decreased mEPSC amplitude in Kv3.3KO contrasts with the increased evoked EPSC amplitude, which the authors interpret as possible synaptic scaling (C95). However, the magnitude of the mEPSC change is small and its functional significance is unclear. The lack of changes in other mEPSC parameters suggests no major postsynaptic alterations.

results.result: Developmental considerations: The calyx of Held undergoes multiple developmental changes including shifts in calcium channel types, myelination, increased Nav1.6 expression, increased presynaptic Kv currents, and changes in postsynaptic AMPAR composition. Despite these changes, Kv3.3 remains crucial for presynaptic function across development (P10-P12 to 6 months).
results.evaluation: Claims C154-C165, C167 are supported by appropriate citations to developmental literature and by the authors' data collected across different ages. The conclusion that Kv3.3 remains important across development (C165) is supported by consistent phenotypes observed at different ages. However, the study does not systematically compare effects at different developmental stages, so age-dependent changes in the magnitude of effects cannot be assessed.

results.result: Kv3 channel assembly and composition: Kv3 channels are regulated by the N-terminal tetramerization domain, do not co-assemble with accessory subunit families, and are likely composed of four Kv3 alpha subunits. Presynaptic Kv3 channels at the calyx of Held require an obligatory Kv3.3 subunit, and Kv3.1 is not required for Kv3.3 localization to the presynaptic membrane.
results.evaluation: Claims C168-C172, C174-C176, C179-C180 combine established knowledge (C168-C172) with inferences from the current data (C174-C176, C179-C180). The conclusion that presynaptic Kv3 channels require Kv3.3 (C174) is strongly supported by the occlusion of TEA effects in Kv3.3KO (Figure 3F-H) and the localization data (Figure 2). The inference that Kv3.1 is not required for Kv3.3 localization (C176) is supported by the presence of Kv3.3 at terminals in Kv3.1KO mice.

results.result: Kv3.3 inactivation properties: Early studies showed N-type inactivation in recombinant Kv3.3, but little or no inactivation is observed at the calyx. This may be due to alternative start codon usage, PKC phosphorylation, or other factors. The lack of inactivating current suggests Kv3.4 subunits are not present in the calyx terminal.
results.evaluation: Claims C181-C184, C186-C189 address the apparent discrepancy between recombinant expression studies and native recordings. The observation of minimal inactivation (C182) is supported by the voltage-clamp data in Figure 1A. The proposed explanations (C183-C184) are supported by appropriate citations. The inference that Kv3.4 is absent (C187) is reasonable given the lack of inactivation and low mRNA levels. The unpublished co-expression data (C188) provides additional support but cannot be fully evaluated.

results.result: Functional implications of Kv3 inactivation: In terminals with inactivating Kv3 currents, cumulative inactivation during high-frequency firing would progressively slow AP repolarization, potentially generating activity-dependent short-term potentiation (as at mossy fiber terminals) or risking earlier transmission failure (as would occur at the calyx). The minimal inactivation at the calyx enables sustained transmission at high frequencies.
results.evaluation: Claims C190-C195 represent logical inferences about the functional consequences of Kv3 inactivation. The comparison to mossy fiber terminals (C192) is supported by citation to Geiger and Jonas, 2000. The inference that inactivation would be detrimental at the calyx (C193) is reasonable given the synapse's requirement for sustained high-frequency transmission. The conclusion that minimal inactivation enables sustained transmission (C195) is a logical inference from the data and the synapse's functional requirements.

results.result: Cytoskeletal interactions and channel localization: Kv3 channel localization is optimized through subunit-specific interactions with cytoskeletal proteins. Ankyrin-G targets Kv3.1b to axons, while ankyrin-R stabilizes both Kv3.1b and Kv3.3 in different compartments. Presynaptic Kv3.3 stabilization likely involves mechanisms beyond ankyrin-R alone, as this would not discriminate between subunits.
results.evaluation: Claims C196-C202 combine established knowledge (C196-C201) with inferences from the current data (C202). The role of ankyrins in Kv3 localization is well-established by the cited literature. The inference that presynaptic Kv3.3 stabilization requires additional mechanisms (C202) is reasonable given the differential presynaptic localization observed in the knockout mice. However, the specific mechanisms remain to be identified.

results.result: Comparison with Wu et al., 2021: The current study demonstrates an ionic role for Kv3.3 at the calyx, showing increased transmitter release and accelerated fast recovery from depression in Kv3.3KO. This contrasts with Wu et al., 2021, which proposed a non-ionic role in endocytosis, but the studies measure different processes over different timescales.
results.evaluation: Claims C204-C209 critically evaluate prior work (Wu et al., 2021) in light of the current findings. The observation that Wu et al. reported similar K+ currents in WT and Kv3.3KO (C204) is inconsistent with the current data showing clear differences. The current study's demonstration of an ionic role (C207) is strongly supported by the AP duration and transmitter release data. The authors appropriately note that their recovery measurements (C208-C209) differ in timescale from the endocytosis measurements in Wu et al., suggesting both ionic and non-ionic mechanisms may coexist.

results.result: Physiological mechanisms and implications: Kv3 channels generate rapid afterhyperpolarization that maximizes calcium driving force and promotes recovery of voltage-gated channels. Short APs permit high firing rates by minimizing the refractory period. At the highest frequencies, neurons switch to firing on alternate stimuli (Phase III), which is impaired in Kv3.3KO. These changes compromise temporal accuracy in sound localization.
results.evaluation: Claims C210-C220 integrate the current findings with established principles of neuronal excitability and auditory processing. The mechanisms described (C210-C213) are supported by appropriate citations and represent established knowledge. The Phase III firing pattern and its impairment in Kv3.3KO (C214-C215) are directly demonstrated in Figure 7. The implications for sound localization (C216-C217) are supported by the in vivo data in Figure 8. The comparison of synaptic delays across studies with different anesthetics (C219-C220) provides important validation of the in vivo approach.

results.result: Broader implications and disease relevance: Kv3.3 is localized to many synaptic terminals across the brain. Disease mutations in Kv3.3, such as SCA13, cause multiple neurological defects that could include aberrant neurotransmitter release. The SCA13 mutation R420H may disrupt interaural level discrimination by reducing gain and signal-to-noise ratio.
results.evaluation: Claims C221, C224-C226 extend the findings to broader contexts and disease implications. The widespread distribution of Kv3.3 (C221) is supported by multiple citations. The general statement about SCA13 causing neurological defects (C224) is established knowledge. However, the specific implications for neurotransmitter release (C225) and the mechanism of R420H mutation effects (C226) are speculative extrapolations from the knockout data. While reasonable hypotheses, these require direct testing in disease models.
